waypoints.name: Bagley Lakes Trailhead / Heather Meadows
waypoints.note: South end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot off SR 542; Northwest Forest Pass required to park, self-issue fee machine at the lot.

waypoints.name: Bagley Lakes
waypoints.note: Trail skirts the Bagley Lakes basin shortly after the trailhead; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Herman Saddle.

waypoints.name: Chain Lakes Trail — leave-trail point for the Herman gully
waypoints.note: Chain Lakes Trail is followed to about 4,500 ft, where climbers peel off trail and start up the gully toward Herman Saddle; no cairns, easy to miss in cloud.

waypoints.name: Herman Saddle
waypoints.note: Broad saddle between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman with views of Baker, Shuksan and Iceberg Lake below; the true col is variously placed anywhere from ~5,300 to ~5,450 ft.

waypoints.name: Heather-and-talus south slope
waypoints.note: Above the saddle you leave any trail and work up loose heather benches and talus on Herman's broad south face — footing is unstable, especially wet or on the descent.

waypoints.name: Unnamed lake / gully to summit ridge
waypoints.note: A small unnamed tarn sits below a series of cirques; a gully rising directly from it leads to the low point on the summit ridge (near-true scramble, easy 3rd class).

waypoints.name: Mount Herman
waypoints.note: Short east ridge gains the summit block from the ridge low point; descend the same south/southwest ridge and heather-scree gully rather than the east side.

itinerary.cal: Best done mid-summer to early fall once the Chain Lakes trail and Herman Saddle slopes are snow-free; a spring/winter ascent is possible on skis or with avalanche gear but is a different, higher-hazard undertaking.

days.note: A short half-day outing: hike the Bagley Lakes/Chain Lakes trail from Heather Meadows up to Herman Saddle, leave the trail near the last switchback to gain the ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman, then follow the south/southwest ridge to the summit. Most parties are back at the car in 4-5 hours.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble via Bagley Lakes and Herman Saddle

schedule.label: Leave Heather Meadows parking lot
schedule.detail: Start on the Bagley Lakes/Chain Lakes trail (~4,400 ft).

schedule.label: Reach Herman Saddle area
schedule.detail: Follow trail roughly 3.5 miles, gaining views toward Mazama Dome and Table Mountain.

schedule.label: Leave trail at last switchback
schedule.detail: Scramble up heather slopes and through scrub trees toward the ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman.

schedule.label: Follow south/southwest ridge to summit
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 scrambling along the ridge, finishing on a short eastern ridge to the true summit (6,285 ft).

schedule.label: Descend via same route
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge and trail back to the trailhead.

days.objective: Summit Mount Herman and return to Heather Meadows trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A single half-day car-to-car scramble: about 4-5 hours round trip, roughly 6 miles and 2,100 ft of gain, no camping required.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate: roughly 3-3.5 miles of trail approach to Herman Saddle area (per Bagley/Chain Lakes trail) plus a few hundred feet of off-trail heather/talus scrambling, ~2,100 ft total gain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light daypack (layers, ice axe if lingering snow, water) - no overnight or technical gear needed

partner_requirements.approachTime: About 1.5-2.5 hours on trail to reach the Herman Saddle area before the off-trail scrambling begins
requiredSkills: Off-trail routefinding through heather and talus
Comfort on loose talus and short exposed scrambling steps (Class 2-3)
Basic snow travel / ice axe use if gullies still hold snow (common into early-mid July)
Turnaround judgment around cliff bands off the standard line
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - comfortable leaving a maintained trail, reading terrain across heather benches and talus, and making a few short exposed Class 3 moves near the summit without a rope

before.approach: Start from the Bagley Lakes Trailhead (~4,200 ft) at the south end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 684.1) south along the eastern shore of Bagley Lake — this is the only reliable water source on the route, and it should still be filtered/treated. At about 0.75 mile, the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 682), which bends east and begins switchbacking up toward Herman Saddle (~5,300 ft), roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,100 ft above the lakes. Snow frequently lingers on this slope into July or even August, and the Forest Service explicitly flags it as avalanche terrain in winter/spring conditions, so check current conditions before an early-season trip; poles and some route-finding are recommended even on the maintained tread. At the last switchback below Herman Saddle — the low point on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome (west) and Mount Herman (east) — leave the maintained trail and go cross-country, climbing open heather slopes and a short band of scrub trees for a couple hundred vertical feet to gain the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge. This off-trail stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach; the correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility. Once on the ridge, follow its crest generally eastward, staying mostly on the south/southwest side over heather benches and loose scree/talus, to the base of a short final east ridge that leads to the true summit at 6,285 ft.

approach_variants.name: Bagley Lakes and Chain Lakes Trail to the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then cross-country to the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Bagley Lakes Trailhead around 4,200 ft, at the south end of the upper Mount Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail #684.1 south along the east shore of Bagley Lake — the only reliable water on the route, and it should still be treated.

At about three quarters of a mile the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail #682, which bends east and switchbacks up toward Herman Saddle at roughly 5,300 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and 1,100 ft above the lakes.

At the last switchback BELOW Herman Saddle, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather and a short band of scrub trees for a couple of hundred vertical feet to gain the connecting ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman.

Then follow the crest generally EAST, staying mostly on the south and southwest side over heather benches and loose scree and talus, to the base of a short final east ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on the slope below Herman Saddle into July or August and the Forest Service flags it as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
hazards: An unmarked exit at the last switchback below the saddle, easy to miss in poor visibility
Lingering snow on the Chain Lakes switchbacks into July or August, flagged as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
Loose down-sloping scree and talus on the connecting ridge, easy to kick onto anyone below
Only one water source, at Bagley Lake, and it needs treating
Two summits on one ridge — Mazama Dome west, Herman east
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE EXIT IS BELOW THE SADDLE, NOT AT IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. You leave Chain Lakes Trail #682 at the LAST SWITCHBACK BELOW Herman Saddle. The correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility and this is the route-finding crux of the day.

SO USE THE SADDLE AS A BACKSTOP RATHER THAN A TARGET. Herman Saddle is the LOW POINT on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome, to the west, and Mount Herman, to the east. If you crest the saddle and the ground starts falling away in front of you toward the Chain Lakes basin, you have gone past your exit — turn round and come back down to the last switchback. That is a reliable test in cloud precisely because a saddle announces itself underfoot.

WHAT YOU CLIMB TO REACH THE RIDGE: open heather slopes and a short band of SCRUB TREES, a couple of hundred vertical feet. Scrub trees at the top of a heather slope is the marker; if you are on scree with nothing growing, you are too high or too far east.

ARRIVAL: you are on the route when you are standing on the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge with a peak at each end of it. From there the direction is EAST, on the south and southwest side of the crest.

THE CLIMBING ITSELF IS THE LAST SHORT EAST RIDGE. Everything before it is heather benches, loose scree and talus. If you have not left your feet by the time the ground runs out ahead of you, you are not at the summit yet; the true top takes a short scramble up that final ridge.

WHICH BUMP IS MAZAMA DOME? It is the WEST end of the same ridge. Turning west out of the saddle area climbs a different, lower feature.

climate.typical: Wet, heavy-snowpack North Cascades maritime climate right at the crest of the range; Heather Meadows sees frequent summer marine cloud/fog. Check the WSDOT SR 542 status and the NWAC forecast before heading up.

bySeason.fall: First snow can arrive by October, quickly shortening the season and icing up the summit ridge.
bySeason.spring: The highway gate near Heather Meadows may not open until May or June in a heavy-snow year, and deep snow lingers in north-facing gullies well into July.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the most reliable snow-free window; afternoon marine cloud and occasional thunderstorms are the main weather hazards.
bySeason.winter: SR 542 is gated well below Heather Meadows, so the peak is instead approached on skis/snowshoes as a much longer backcountry tour with real avalanche exposure — The Mountaineers rate this terrain 'Challenging.'

pro_tips: Buy or verify your Northwest Forest Pass ahead of time at the Glacier Public Service Center — the trailhead iron ranger doesn't always have change.
Start early: the Heather Meadows lot fills on summer weekends and afternoon cloud frequently socks in the basin.
Backcountry skiers approach very differently in winter/spring, starting from the lower winter-closure gate — that's a much longer, avalanche-exposed tour, not this summer scramble.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the end of maintained FS-3065; the rough road continues ~2 more miles toward Twin Lakes, passable to high-clearance vehicles.
waypoints.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road (FS 3065) to the end of the maintained grade, where a self-issue kiosk takes the Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee. The road is snow-gated through winter and spring. Above this point it degrades for roughly two more miles toward Twin Lakes and the Forest Service recommends high clearance, so many parties leave the car here and walk the rest.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp at the alpine lake basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains; last reliable water before the high traverse to Low and High Passes.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the rough upper road about two miles and roughly 1,500 feet of gain, on foot or in a high-clearance vehicle, to the lake basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains. Fill water here. These lakes are the last reliable source before the high traverse to Low and High Passes, and there is nothing dependable past High Pass in late season.

waypoints.name: Low Pass
waypoints.note: Trail contours Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and drops through Low Pass before climbing again toward High Pass; boot path is easy to lose here in fog or lingering snow.
waypoints.directions: From the lakes follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) about half a mile to a signed junction. The left branch climbs to the Winchester lookout, so take the right fork onto the High Pass Trail (#676). It runs through meadows across Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and crosses an avalanche chute where steep, exposed snow can hang on into August, then reaches the notch of Low Pass. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it while that chute still holds snow, and expect to lose the boot path through the pass itself in fog or lingering snow.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Basin-facing pass with the first close views of Larrabee's south face; leave the maintained High Pass Trail here and traverse cross-country toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Climb again out of Low Pass on the High Pass Trail, a little over half a mile and about 300 feet of gain, passing the tailings and ruins of the old Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is a scenic but wind-exposed spot with the first close look at Larrabee's south face. It is also the end of the maintained trail.

waypoints.name: South Ridge crossing / SW Face gullies
waypoints.note: Boot up ~40-degree scree/snow slopes to cross the south ridge onto the southwest-face gully system; Larrabee's rock is notoriously loose and crumbly, so a helmet is essential.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the unmarked climbers' path as it contours and drops 100 to 200 feet northwest into the basin under Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band near 6,400 feet. Cross boulder fields and then scree and dirt, booting up steep ground to the southwest spur at about 6,900 feet. Cairns mark parts of this but they sit far apart and the way trail vanishes for long stretches, and boot paths here can pull you toward the East Ridge, so hold to the south and southwest side of the peak.

waypoints.name: Mount Larrabee Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,865 ft), 1.4 mi south of the Canada–US border; descend by reversing the south ridge/gully system back through the scree basin to High Pass.
waypoints.directions: From the spur, find the gully system cut into the rock face: two narrow parallel channels about thirty feet apart, of which the right-hand one is the line. It starts tight and opens into broken rock, Class 3 to 4 on loose phyllite, and holds steep snow into July and sometimes August. Climb it one person at a time with helmets on, since anything knocked loose runs straight down onto whoever is below. It tops out on the crest of the south ridge; follow the crest to the summit, favoring the west side and the firmer rock of the rib over the gully floor, with a faint way trail and scattered cairns coming and going.

itinerary.cal: Twin Lakes Rd (FS 3065) can be rough or seasonally gated below the lakes, and the gully often holds snow into July, favoring an ice axe/microspikes for early-season attempts.

days.note: From the Twin Lakes trailhead, follow the High Pass trail north over Low Pass and High Pass, then leave the trail around 6,400 ft and traverse/descend slightly into the basin below Larrabee's south face. Scramble scree and boulders to a gully system at ~6,900 ft (take the right-hand of two narrow chutes), climb loose rock to gain the south ridge, then follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) to the summit. Descend by reversing the route — the loose, chossy rock makes the descent nearly as slow as the ascent, and a helmet is considered mandatory due to rockfall.
days.title: Twin Lakes to summit and back, car-to-car

schedule.label: Leave trailhead area
schedule.detail: Twin Lakes Rd is rough/rutted and sometimes gated below the lakes; if impassable, park near Yellow Aster Butte TH, adding ~2.3 mi and 500 ft each way.

schedule.label: Twin Lakes, start High Pass trail
schedule.detail: Head north past the lakes toward Low Pass then High Pass.

schedule.label: Leave trail, enter south-face basin
schedule.detail: Around 6,400 ft, traverse and drop slightly into the basin facing Larrabee's south side.

schedule.label: Ascend the gully
schedule.detail: At ~6,900 ft find the two narrow parallel chutes; take the right-hand one, staying climber's right on better rock, to broken terrain and the ridge crest.

schedule.label: Summit (7,865 ft)
schedule.detail: Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the top.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the full route; loose rock makes downclimbing the gully slow and rockfall-prone.

days.objective: Summit Mount Larrabee via the South Ridge gully

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: roughly 10 miles round trip with about 4,200 ft of gain, typically 7-9 hours including a slow, loose descent; strong parties have done it in 6, casual parties closer to 9-10.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strenuous full day; roughly 6 miles and significant elevation gain if done car-to-car, or a shorter summit push if camped at Twin Lakes
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack for the summit push; overnight pack if establishing the Twin Lakes camp described in the beta

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~2-3 hrs hiking in to Twin Lakes/High Pass area for a day trip; multi-day parties hike in and camp at Twin Lakes first, then face a shorter (~6 hr) summit day
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, blocky rock
Route-finding on ridge and gully terrain (staying on the more solid rib, avoiding the looser gully)
Rockfall awareness and helmet use - small party size recommended to reduce rockfall risk to others
Basic snow travel/kick-stepping for lingering early-season snow near the ridge
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate to advanced scrambler; prior Class 3-4 scrambling experience strongly recommended given sustained loose rock and summit exposure

before.permit: Free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
